\begin{abstract}
Recursive Bayesian estimation---the Kalman filter and its nonlinear, robust,
and adaptive descendants---underlies inertial navigation, sensor fusion,
robotics, and multi-object tracking. Yet the gap between the elegant textbook
recursion and software that is numerically stable, maintainable, and usable in
a deployed system is wide, and is rarely discussed in the estimation
literature. This paper treats the \emph{engineering} of such software as a
first-class problem. We (i) frame filtering, smoothing, and multi-target
tracking in a single Bayesian notation so that implementation decisions map to
one shared vocabulary; (ii) catalogue the recurring failure modes---loss of
covariance positive-definiteness, near-singular inverses, brittle
interfaces, and evaluation that cannot be reproduced---and the defenses against
them; (iii) argue for a small set of design patterns (a uniform filter
interface, pluggable sigma-point strategies, ready-made model builders, and a
factory for switching strategies) that let a single codebase span a dozen
algorithms without duplicating application code; and (iv) describe a
validation methodology based on normalized-innovation and normalized-estimation
error consistency statistics rather than point estimates alone. Throughout, we
illustrate the discussion with a freely available reference implementation.
The result is a checklist, grounded in both theory and practice, for building
or evaluating a state-estimation and tracking toolkit.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Kalman filter, recursive Bayesian estimation, sensor fusion, multi-object
tracking, data association, numerical software, software design
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}

The Kalman filter~\cite{kalman1960} is the canonical solution to online
estimation of the state of a linear system from noisy measurements. Its
successors---the extended Kalman filter (EKF), unscented Kalman filter
(UKF)~\cite{julier2004unscented}, cubature Kalman filter
(CKF)~\cite{arasaratnam2009cubature}, particle filters, and a long tail of
robust and adaptive variants---push the same predict/update recursion to
nonlinear dynamics, non-Gaussian noise, and hostile operating conditions.
Applications include attitude determination, GPS/IMU fusion, robotics, and
multi-target tracking in radar and vision.

A practitioner implementing these algorithms quickly discovers that the
textbook recursion is the \emph{easy} part. The hard problems are numerical:
covariances must remain symmetric positive-definite over long horizons;
innovation covariances become near-singular under poor observability; and
subtle indexing conventions for block-diagonal state vectors turn correct
math into silently wrong estimates. A second class of problems is
architectural: a library that exposes twenty filters but no common interface
forces application code to be rewritten for each one, and a library whose
interfaces are convenient only for the author's original use case will not
survive contact with real data. A third class is methodological: how do we
know a filter is working at all, and how do we compare implementations
honestly?

This paper organizes the accumulated answers to these questions into a
coherent, largely framework-agnostic treatment, so that a reader can apply
the advice to any language or library. Our contributions are:

\begin{enumerate}
\item a unified Bayesian formulation of filtering, smoothing, and multi-target
tracking with consistent notation (Section~\ref{sec:formulation});
\item a taxonomy of algorithm families and the numerical/operational failure
modes each one introduces (Sections~\ref{sec:taxonomy}
and~\ref{sec:engineering});
\item a small set of software design patterns that have proven sufficient to
keep a broad algorithm suite maintainable and uniform
(Section~\ref{sec:patterns});
\item a validation and evaluation methodology grounded in filter consistency
statistics and reproducible, honest benchmarks (Section~\ref{sec:validation});
\item two short case studies---attitude estimation from an inertial
measurement unit and multi-target tracking of pedestrians in real video---that
exercise the full pipeline (Section~\ref{sec:case-studies}).
\end{enumerate}

We deliberately keep the exposition framework-agnostic; where a concrete
reference implementation helps, we point to \toolkit{}, an open-source
(Apache-2.0) library written in Python and NumPy, whose public interface and
tests instantiate every pattern and validation idea below.

\section{Problem Formulation}
\label{sec:formulation}

\subsection{Recursive Bayesian filtering}

Let $x_k \in \mathbb{R}^n$ be the state at discrete time $k$ and $z_k \in
\mathbb{R}^m$ a measurement. A dynamic system is described by a transition
density and a measurement density,
\begin{equation}
x_k \sim p(x_k \mid x_{k-1}), \qquad
z_k \sim p(z_k \mid x_k).
\end{equation}
Filtering maintains the posterior $p(x_k \mid z_{1:k})$ through two steps.
The \emph{prediction} applies the Chapman--Kolmogorov equation,
\begin{equation}
p(x_k \mid z_{1:k-1}) = \int p(x_k \mid x_{k-1})\,
p(x_{k-1} \mid z_{1:k-1})\, dx_{k-1},
\end{equation}
and the \emph{update} applies Bayes' rule,
\begin{equation}
p(x_k \mid z_{1:k}) \propto p(z_k \mid x_k)\,
p(x_k \mid z_{1:k-1}).
\label{eq:bayes}
\end{equation}
Every filter in this paper is a different way of representing the two
densities in \eqref{eq:bayes}: moments for the Kalman filter and its
Gaussian variants, a particle set for sequential Monte Carlo, and so on.

For linear-Gaussian models, $x_k = F x_{k-1} + w_k$, $z_k = H x_k + v_k$
with $w_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0,Q)$ and $v_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0,R)$, the
posterior is Gaussian and is propagated exactly by the Kalman filter,
\begin{align}
\hat{x}_{k\mid k-1} &= F \hat{x}_{k-1},\qquad
P_{k\mid k-1} = F P_{k-1} F^{\top} + Q, \\
y_k &= z_k - H\hat{x}_{k\mid k-1}, \qquad
S_k = H P_{k\mid k-1} H^{\top} + R, \\
K_k &= P_{k\mid k-1} H^{\top} S_k^{-1}, \\
\hat{x}_k &= \hat{x}_{k\mid k-1} + K_k y_k, \\
P_k &= (I - K_k H) P_{k\mid k-1}.
\end{align}
The residual $y_k$ (innovation) and its covariance $S_k$ are central: their
statistics are the primary diagnostic instrument for filter health.

\subsection{Nonlinear and non-Gaussian extensions}

When the dynamics or measurement model are nonlinear, $x_k = f(x_{k-1}) +
w_k$, $z_k = h(x_k) + v_k$, no closed-form posterior exists in general. Three
approximation families dominate:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Linearization (EKF).} Taylor-expand $f$ and $h$ around the
current estimate and run the linear recursion with Jacobians
$F_k=\partial f/\partial x$ and $H_k=\partial h/\partial x$. Cheap, but
breaks down when the true posterior is not captured by the local linearization.
When Jacobians are unavailable or error-prone, a central finite-difference
Jacobian is a pragmatic, testable substitute.
\item \textbf{Deterministic sampling (UKF, CKF).} Approximate the
distribution by a small set of weighted points propagated through the exact
nonlinearity---no Jacobians required. The unscented transform places
$2n+1$ sigma points and is accurate to second order; the cubature rule uses
$2n$ points and scales better in high dimensions~\cite{arasaratnam2009cubature}.
\item \textbf{Stochastic sampling (particle filters).} Represent the
posterior by $N$ weighted particles, giving an asymptotically exact
approximation for arbitrary, possibly multimodal, non-Gaussian posteriors.
Rao--Blackwellization marginalizes any conditionally linear substate, trading
particle count for closed-form Kalman updates.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Smoothing and parameter learning}

A filter is causal; a \emph{smoother} additionally conditions on future
measurements. The Rauch--Tung--Striebel (RTS) smoother~\cite{rauch1965maximum}
runs the filter forward and a correction pass backward, and is the workhorse
for offline estimation (mapping, trajectory post-processing, EM). Fixed-lag
smoothing bounds the backward horizon for near-online use.

The same machinery supports \emph{learning}: if the model structure $F,H$ is
known but the noise covariances $Q,R$ are not, expectation--maximization
fits them by alternating the forward/backward pass (E-step) with a
covariance update from the smoothed sufficient statistics
(M-step)~\cite{shumway1982}. A cheaper, online alternative adapts $Q,R$ so
that the innovation statistics match their theoretical distribution, which
connects directly to the consistency diagnostics of
Section~\ref{sec:validation}.

\subsection{Multi-object tracking}

Multiple targets require not only filtering but \emph{data association}: which
measurement belongs to which track, and which measurements are clutter. The
canonical lightweight design---popularized as SORT~\cite{bewley2016sort}---is
a bank of Kalman filters plus per-frame assignment:
\begin{enumerate}
\item predict each existing track;
\item build a cost matrix (e.g.\ squared Mahalanobis distance using each
track's innovation covariance) and solve the assignment with the Hungarian
algorithm under a gating threshold;
\item update matched tracks, age out unmatched ones, and instantiate tentative
new tracks for unmatched detections;
\item confirm a track only after $n_{\mathrm{init}}$ consecutive matches and
delete it after $N_{\max}$ misses.
\end{enumerate}
Joint probabilistic data association (JPDA) and Poisson multi-Bernoulli
mixture (PMBM) filters generalize this to principled treatment of clutter and
track uncertainty, at higher computational and conceptual cost. All three
share the same building blocks: per-target filters, an innovation
covariance, and a gate. This is why a filtering library and a tracking
library are naturally two layers of the same design rather than separate
products.

\section{An Algorithmic Taxonomy}
\label{sec:taxonomy}

A library author must decide \emph{which} algorithms to implement and, more
importantly, how a user should choose among them. The decision tree that has
proved durable in practice is:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Linear, Gaussian} $\rightarrow$ Kalman filter. Use the
square-root or information form when numerics or many sensors demand it.
\item \textbf{Nonlinear} $\rightarrow$ EKF if Jacobians are easy and the
nonlinearity is mild; otherwise UKF/CKF (no derivatives).
\item \textbf{Non-Gaussian / multimodal} $\rightarrow$ particle filter;
Rao--Blackwellized particle filter if the model is partially linear.
\item \textbf{Maneuvering targets} $\rightarrow$ interacting multiple models
(IMM): run several filters with different process models in parallel and
blend them by model likelihood. A cheap alternative is a fading-memory filter
that inflates the predicted covariance by a factor $>1$ to discount stale
data.
\item \textbf{Unknown noise statistics} $\rightarrow$ adaptive filtering,
EM, or innovation-based auto-tuning.
\item \textbf{Multiple targets} $\rightarrow$ per-target filters plus an
association layer (SORT/JPDA/PMBM).
\item \textbf{Adversarial or uncertain models} $\rightarrow$ $H_\infty$
filtering, which minimizes worst-case estimation error rather than assuming
known noise.
\end{itemize}

The critical insight for software design is that nearly all of these are
variations on the same $\texttt{predict}/\texttt{update}$ contract; only the
innards differ. That observation, more than any individual algorithm, drives
the architecture of Section~\ref{sec:patterns}.

\section{Engineering a Filter Is Not the Same as Writing One}
\label{sec:engineering}

Five concerns separate a working demo from software that survives deployment.

\subsection{Numerical stability}

The textbook update $P_k = (I-KH)P_{k-1}$ is algebraically correct but
numerically fragile: round-off can make $P$ lose symmetry and, worse,
positive-definiteness, after which a Cholesky factorization or a
log-likelihood evaluation fails or silently produces nonsense. Durable
defenses, in increasing order of sophistication, are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item the Joseph form
$P_k = (I-KH)P_{k-1}(I-KH)^{\top} + K R K^{\top}$, which is guaranteed
positive semi-definite for any gain;
\item explicit symmetrization $P \leftarrow (P+P^{\top})/2$ after every
covariance update;
\item \emph{condition-aware} inversion. Plain $\mathrm{inv}(S)$ returns
garbage without raising for near-singular $S$; checking the condition number
and falling back to a regularized or pseudo-inverse gives predictable
behavior instead of silent corruption;
\item square-root forms that propagate the Cholesky factor of $P$
directly, keeping the covariance implicitly positive-definite by
construction.
\end{enumerate}
A reference implementation should apply these policies \emph{uniformly}
through one shared linear-algebra helper rather than ad hoc in each filter.

\subsection{Determinism and reproducibility}

Filters are increasingly used inside evaluation harnesses and learned
pipelines. Seedable, isolated random streams (per-constructor random number
generators that do not perturb global state) make particle and ensemble
methods reproducible; giving every algorithmic constant a single home (one
module-level constants registry) makes tuning repeatable.

\subsection{State conventions}

Batched or multi-axis states invite ordering bugs. A library that fixes one
convention---e.g.\ block-per-axis layout ``$[\text{axis}_1,\; v_1,\;
\text{axis}_2,\; v_2,\ldots]$''---and expresses all model builders
(``constant velocity'', ``constant turn'', ``measurement of position'')
through that convention eliminates an entire class of silent errors and makes
the corresponding tests trivial to write.

\subsection{Irregular data}

Real streams drop measurements, arrive asynchronously, or arrive out of order.
A filter API should therefore treat ``predict-only'' steps as first-class
(no measurement this tick), support batch processing over sequences with an
explicit ``missing'' sentinel, and offer an out-of-sequence-measurement buffer
for multi-rate sensors.

\subsection{Optional dependencies}

A modern estimation library will want DataFrame and scikit-learn
integrations, terminal demos, plotting, and (sometimes) PyTorch. None of
these belong in the core dependency set; the core should import only the
numerics stack, with integrations loaded lazily or behind extras.

\section{Design Patterns}
\label{sec:patterns}

The following five patterns, each simple in isolation, compose into a library
that can host a dozen algorithms without forking application code.

\subsection{A uniform filter interface}

Define one abstract filter with the two essential operations and a handful of
secondary conveniences,
\begin{lstlisting}
class Filter(ABC):
    def predict(self, dt=1.0, **kw): ...
    def update(self, measurement, **kw): ...
    def measure(self, state=None): ...       # state -> measurement space
    def predict_only(self, dt=1.0, **kw): ...
    def reset(self, state=None, covariance=None): ...
    def filter_sequence(self, measurements, dt=1.0, missing=None): ...
\end{lstlisting}
Because every filter---linear, nonlinear, particle-based, or information
form---obeys the same contract, a user can swap a Kalman filter for an
adaptive or square-root variant by changing one line, and the entire
higher-level machinery (tracking, tuning, DataFrame integration, diagnostics)
works unchanged.

\subsection{Strategy objects for pluggable internals}

Hard-coding one sigma-point rule inside the UKF prevents experimentation.
Factoring the rule into a small strategy object
(\texttt{SimplexSigmaPoints}, \texttt{MerweScaledSigmaPoints},
\texttt{JulierSigmaPoints}) lets a single filter implementation expose every
variant through constructor injection. The same idea recurs for measurement
gates and association algorithms.

\subsection{Ready-made model builders}

Users should not re-derive $F$, $Q$, $H$, $R$ by hand for the standard
motion/measurement families. A small set of parameterized builders
(constant-velocity, constant-acceleration, coordinated-turn, position
measurement) returns the matrices consistent with the library's state
convention, so a ``correct'' model is obtained by construction and every
documented example shares it.

\subsection{A factory for strategy selection}

String-based construction (\texttt{mode="ekf"}, \texttt{mode="ukf"}, \dots)
lets configuration files, CLIs, and hyperparameter sweeps choose filters
without importing them. It also gives integration layers (a
scikit-learn-style estimator, a command-line benchmark) a single entry point.

\subsection{Procedural alongside object-oriented}

Many users come from FilterPy-style code and want functions
($\texttt{predict}(x,P,F,Q)$ returning the new pair) as much as stateful
objects. Exposing both on top of the same math is cheap and dramatically
widens adoption; one should be a thin wrapper over the other so they cannot
drift apart.

\subsection{Batching as an implementation detail}

When $N$ independent series must be filtered (many tracked objects, many
replicates), a naive per-series loop wastes the vectorized hardware.
A \emph{vectorized filter} that broadcasts every matrix operation over a
leading batch axis delivers large speedups while preserving the uniform
interface---users switch \texttt{KalmanFilter} to a batched subclass, not to a
separate library.

\section{Validation and Evaluation}
\label{sec:validation}

\subsection{Consistency statistics beat point estimates}

A single RMSE number cannot distinguish a well-tuned filter from a lucky one.
The standard theory-backed diagnostics are the normalized innovation squared
(NIS) and normalized estimation error squared (NEES). For a consistent
filter, each is chi-squared distributed with, respectively, $m$ and $n$
degrees of freedom~\cite{bar2011estimation}:
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{NIS}_k = y_k^{\top} S_k^{-1} y_k \sim \chi^2_m, \qquad
\mathrm{NEES}_k = e_k^{\top} P_k^{-1} e_k \sim \chi^2_n,
\end{equation}
where $e_k = x_k - \hat{x}_k$ uses the true state (available in simulation or
with ground truth). Averaging NIS/NEES over a run and comparing against the
expected value detects over- and under-confidence; the innovation
autocorrelation (whiteness test) detects model mismatch. Consistency tests
should be first-class library functions, because they are exactly what a
developer needs when tuning $Q$ and $R$---and they are the theoretical basis
for the innovation-based auto-tuners of Section~\ref{sec:formulation}.

\subsection{Reproducible, honest benchmarks}

Benchmarks are only useful if the task, the data, and the reference
implementations are public and the results are reported without cherry-picking.
Concretely: fix one task (same $F,Q,H,R$, same measurement sequence), compare
against reference libraries on identical inputs, and report \emph{both} the
case the new library wins and the case it loses. In our reference suite, a
purpose-built vectorized filter outperforms a dedicated batching library by
roughly $4\times$ on 1{,}000 concurrent series, while a minimal single-purpose
library still has lower per-call overhead for one bare filter loop---both
results are worth stating, because they tell different users different truths.

\subsection{Testing the math}

Regression tests should include cross-checks between algebraically equivalent
implementations (e.g.\ square-root vs.\ standard Kalman filter must agree to
machine precision), closed-form one-step numerical answers, analytic vs.\
finite-difference Jacobians, and stress cases (zero time step, extreme noise,
exactly singular innovation covariance). These tests are the real
documentation of numerical policy.

\section{Case Studies}
\label{sec:case-studies}

\subsection{Attitude estimation from an inertial measurement unit}

A common, instructive problem: estimate orientation from a gyroscope
(process: integrate angular velocity) corrected by an accelerometer
(measurement: the direction of gravity in the body frame). With a unit
quaternion $q=[w,x,y,z]^{\top}$ as the state, a constant-angular-velocity
step integrates to a delta quaternion and the process model is the quaternion
product, which is \emph{linear} in the state---its Jacobian is the exact
right-multiplication matrix of the delta quaternion, not an approximation.
Two lessons recur. First, observability: gravity alone cannot observe yaw;
without a magnetometer or course measurement, yaw noise random-walks
uncorrected. Second, naive quaternion-state EKFs linearize only locally, so
over-aggressive measurement noise assumptions cause the corrected state to
leave the unit manifold before renormalization; the documented remedy
(inflate the assumed $R$ modestly) is precisely the kind of hard-won tuning
knowledge that belongs in a library's documentation and tests, not in the head
of its author. A general treatment of quaternion kinematics is given
in~\cite{sola2017quaternion}.

\subsection{Pedestrian multi-target tracking in real video}

To exercise the whole stack, we track pedestrians in the public MOT16
benchmark sequence \texttt{MOT16-02}~\cite{mot16}: each ground-truth box
$[x_1,y_1,x_2,y_2]$ is treated as a four-axis measurement and fed to the
per-corner constant-velocity bank with gated Hungarian association. The
tracker keeps stable identities through brief occlusions and confirms tracks
only after consecutive detections; overlaying the filtered boxes on the real
frames makes association behavior legible in a way that synthetic data cannot.
The same tracker, fed by a YOLO detector instead of ground truth, becomes a
real-time vehicle/person tracker; the only change is the source of the boxes.
This underlines the layering argument of Section~\ref{sec:formulation}: the
filtering core never needs to know what produced the measurements.

\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{FilterPy} provides pedagogical, textbook-faithful implementations
of the KF/EKF/UKF family and an RTS smoother, with no shared abstract base
across all filters and little recent maintenance. It remains the clearest
reference for learning the equations.

\paragraph{pykalman} offers a compact filter/smooth/EM interface in the
scikit-learn idiom, restricted to the linear-Gaussian model.

\paragraph{simdkalman} vectorizes the linear KF across a leading axis---a
narrow, well-executed contribution with no nonlinear or tracking support.

\paragraph{Stone Soup} is a component-based research framework from the
defence community covering the full tracking pipeline (hypothesisers,
associators, metrics) at a much higher conceptual cost than a library whose
users mostly need ``fuse a GPS fix with an accelerometer.''

\paragraph{Differentiable filters} (e.g.\ JAX-based Kalman smoothing) target
learning-based pipelines and assume the user adopts the autodiff ecosystem
wholesale.

The common thread relevant to this paper is that none of these systems treats
numerical-stability policy, consistency diagnostics, and interface uniformity
as parts of the same design problem---which is the gap this paper addresses.

\section{Discussion and Conclusion}

Recursive estimation is easy to implement and hard to operationalize. This
paper has argued that the hard parts are systematically addressable: a uniform
Bayesian formulation keeps the algorithm space navigable; condition-aware
numerics and square-root forms prevent the silent failures that plague naive
implementations; five modest design patterns keep a broad algorithm suite
maintainable; and consistency statistics, rather than point metrics, provide
the feedback loop that makes tuning and evaluation scientific. We have
illustrated each point with a freely available reference implementation
(the \toolkit{} library), whose public interface, model builders, and test
suite instantiate the advice above and whose MOT16 case study runs on real
pedestrian footage.

Two limitations deserve restatement. First, a deterministic
sigma-point/particle-free stack has no GPU/autodiff backend; gradient-based
noise learning and large-scale parallel filtering remain a separate,
parallel implementation surface. Second, strict static typing across a
long-lived numerical codebase---particularly narrowing
$\texttt{Optional[np.ndarray]}$ attributes on the base filter---is valuable
but must be retrofitted incrementally rather than assumed. We consider both
honest statements of scope rather than defects.

\section*{Availability}
The reference implementation used throughout is released under the Apache
License 2.0, installable from PyPI and available at
\url{https://github.com/LakoreAI/kalbee}, with documentation at
\url{https://lakoreai.github.io/kalbee}. Data for the pedestrian case study is
from the MOT Challenge~\cite{mot16} (\url{https://motchallenge.net}); a small
fetcher script downloads only the needed sequence.
